title: SAMSON KILLED 1,000 MEN WITH A DONKEY’S JAWBONE—BUT THE MOST DANGEROUS ENEMY WAS STILL INSIDE HIM
paragraphs: SAMSON KILLED 1,000 MEN WITH A DONKEY’S JAWBONE—BUT THE MOST DANGEROUS ENEMY WAS STILL INSIDE HIM

He walked away from a battlefield covered with a thousand fallen enemies. Yet the story of Samson reveals something terrifying: you can defeat what is standing against you while remaining vulnerable to what is living inside you.
There are Bible stories we have heard so many times that we stop feeling how shocking they actually are.
Samson and the jawbone of a donkey is one of them.
We picture the strong man. The impossible weapon. The overwhelming enemy. The astonishing victory.
One man.
One jawbone.
One thousand Philistines.
But slow the scene down.
Because Judges 15 is not a superhero movie.

It is the story of a deeply complicated man living in a deeply broken generation, empowered by the Spirit of God for a divine purpose while repeatedly displaying impulses that would eventually contribute to his destruction.
And somewhere inside Samson’s scandalous story is a warning for every person who has ever mistaken spiritual usefulness for spiritual health.
You can be gifted and still be wounded.
You can experience victory and still have dangerous appetites.
You can be used by God and still desperately need God.
You can defeat a thousand enemies in public...
and still lose battles nobody sees.
That is why Samson’s story matters.
And that is why you should not rush past the jawbone.

The moment begins after Samson has been bound and delivered into the hands of the Philistines. His own countrymen from Judah have tied him with new ropes because they fear the Philistines ruling over them.
Imagine that humiliation.
The man appointed to begin delivering Israel is handed over by Israelites themselves.
Then the Philistines see him.
They come shouting.
The ropes are around his arms.
The enemy believes the fight is already over.
And then Scripture says something far more important than the size of Samson’s muscles.
Judges 15:14 says:
“The Spirit of the LORD came powerfully upon him.”
The Hebrew expression is:
וַתִּצְלַח עָלָיו רוּחַ יְהוָה
Vattitzlach alav Ruach YHWH.
The verb commonly transliterated tsalach carries the sense here of rushing upon, coming powerfully upon, or empowering.
That changes the entire scene.
The theological center of the story is not:
“Look how strong Samson was.”
It is:
Look what happened when the Spirit of the LORD empowered the deliverer God had chosen.
The ropes on Samson’s arms become like burned flax. His restraints fall away.
Then he sees something lying nearby.
Not a sword.
Not a spear.
Not military armor.
Not the weapon anyone would choose before confronting an army.
A donkey’s jawbone.
Judges 15:15 records:
וַיִּמְצָא לְחִי־חֲמוֹר טְרִיָּה וַיִּשְׁלַח יָדוֹ וַיִּקָּחֶהָ וַיַּךְ־בָּהּ אֶלֶף אִישׁ
Vayyimtsa lechi-chamor teriyyah, vayyishlach yado vayyiqqacheha, vayyakh-bah elef ish.
In context:
“He found a fresh jawbone of a donkey, reached out his hand and took it, and struck down a thousand men with it.”
A thousand men.
With the jawbone of a donkey.
And Samson celebrates the victory with Hebrew wordplay preserved in Judges 15:16:

בִּלְחִי הַחֲמוֹר חֲמוֹר חֲמֹרָתָיִם
בִּלְחִי הַחֲמוֹר הִכֵּיתִי אֶלֶף אִישׁ
The line plays on the similar sounds of chamor, “donkey,” and chamor/chamorathayim, language associated with heaps or piled heaps.
English translations render the wordplay somewhat differently because its sound and force cannot be reproduced perfectly in English.
The basic sense is unmistakable:
“With the jawbone of a donkey... I have struck down a thousand men.”
It is brutal.
It is astonishing.
And it is easy to make Samson the hero.
But Judges refuses to give us such a simple character.
Samson is a deliverer, yes.
He was set apart from the womb.
God truly empowered him.
God truly used him against the Philistines.
But Samson is not Jesus.
That distinction matters enormously.
Samson is morally complicated.
Impulsive.
Often driven by personal desire.
Capable of tremendous acts under divine empowerment while simultaneously demonstrating catastrophic weaknesses of character.
And perhaps that is why his story gets uncomfortably close to us.
Because some of us know what it is like to look strong while something inside us is starving.
People see your victories.
God sees your thirst.
People see the ministry.
God sees the secret.
People see the marriage photos.
God sees the distance between you.
People see the Bible verses you post.
God sees what you search for when nobody is watching.
People hear you say, “God is good.”
God hears the thoughts you are afraid to say out loud.
People see someone who survived.
God sees someone exhausted from surviving.
And perhaps you have become incredibly skilled at killing the enemies everyone can see while feeding the enemy nobody can see.
Samson could stand against an army.
But Samson struggled to govern Samson.
Read that again.
A man powerful enough to leave a thousand enemies defeated could still be endangered by his own desires.
That should humble every Christian with a platform.
Every pastor.
Every leader.
Every parent.
Every husband.
Every wife.
Every worshiper.
Every person who knows how to look spiritually strong.
Giftedness is not the same thing as godliness.
A spiritual experience is not permission to stop pursuing holiness.
Yesterday’s victory does not make today’s temptation harmless.
And being used by God does not mean there are no areas of your life that desperately need repentance.
But something happens immediately after Samson’s astonishing victory that exposes another side of him.
He becomes desperately thirsty.
The warrior who just defeated a thousand men suddenly realizes he cannot even provide himself with water.
That detail is breathtaking.
Samson cries to the LORD in Judges 15:18:
“You have given your servant this great victory. Must I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?”
There it is.
The strong man is thirsty.
The victorious man is desperate.
The man who just held a jawbone now has to pray.
And perhaps that is one of the most important images in Samson’s entire story.
Because eventually every strong person discovers something.
There are needs strength cannot satisfy.
There are wounds success cannot heal.
There are sins discipline alone cannot erase.
There is guilt achievement cannot silence.
There is a thirst this world cannot quench.
You can win the promotion and still be thirsty.
Build the business and still be thirsty.
Grow the platform and still be thirsty.
Get married and still be thirsty.
Become admired and still be thirsty.
Have thousands of followers and still go to bed feeling completely unknown.
You can even serve in church...
and still be thirsty.
The answer is not another jawbone.
The answer is not another victory.
The answer is not becoming more impressive.
You need living water.
And this is where Samson’s story begins pointing beyond Samson.
Centuries later, another Deliverer would come.
But He would be nothing like Samson.
Samson repeatedly moved through cycles of retaliation.
Jesus Christ willingly absorbed violence and injustice and went to the cross.
Samson killed his enemies.
Jesus prayed for His executioners.
Samson needed deliverance himself.
Jesus is the sinless Deliverer.
Samson stretched out his arms and brought death to his enemies.
Jesus stretched out His arms on a cross and willingly gave His life so His enemies could become His family.
That is the scandal of grace.
The Gospel does not announce that good people can improve themselves enough for God.
The Gospel announces that sinners who could never rescue themselves can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
We have sinned.
Not merely “made mistakes.”
Sinned.
We have loved things God hates.
Hidden things.
Excused things.
Worshiped ourselves.
Used people.
Fed pride.
Carried bitterness.
Entertained lust.
Clung to unforgiveness.
Pretended.
And no amount of religious performance can erase our guilt.
But Jesus came.
The eternal Son of God entered our brokenness, lived without sin, died for sinners, and rose again.
At the cross, justice and mercy meet.
Sin is not treated as insignificant.
It is so serious that Christ bears its judgment.
Yet sinners are not declared unreachable.
Grace reaches them through Christ.
That means your scandal does not have to become the final sentence of your life.
Your worst night does not have to own your eternity.
Your addiction does not get the last word.
Your pornography does not get the last word.
Your adultery does not get the last word.
Your bitterness does not get the last word.
Your shame does not get the last word.
Your failure does not get the last word.
Jesus does.
But grace is not permission to continue comfortably in rebellion.
Grace calls us out of hiding.
Jesus does not merely forgive us so we can remain chained to the things destroying us.
He calls us to repent, believe, follow Him, and walk in newness of life.
Repentance is not purchasing forgiveness with good behavior.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior because God’s grace has confronted us with the truth.
And maybe this is where the story stopped being about Samson.
Maybe it became about you.
What is your jawbone?
What is the visible victory you keep pointing toward because you do not want anyone examining the invisible battle?
What have you conquered publicly while secretly refusing to surrender privately?
Maybe everyone thinks you are strong.
But you are thirsty.
Maybe everyone thinks your marriage is fine.
But you know something is dying.
Maybe people call you faithful.
But your private browser history tells another story.
Maybe you sing worship songs with tears in your eyes while carrying resentment you refuse to release.
Maybe you preach grace to everybody except yourself.
Maybe you have spent years running from God because you believe what you did was simply too ugly.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not to become a better Samson.
The answer is Jesus.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Stop negotiating with the thing crucifying your intimacy with God.
Stop protecting the secret that is poisoning you.
You do not need another performance.
You need surrender.
Be honest.
And believers reading those words—do not attack the wounded.
Pray.
Encourage.
Point people toward Jesus.
Let the comment section become something rarer than another internet argument.
Let it become a place where people remember they are not the only ones fighting.
Because somebody reading this tonight may be one prayer away from finally admitting, “I need help.”
Somebody may need your testimony.
Somebody may need to know Christ is still restoring people.
Not because typing a phrase saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
And please understand something else.
Not because sharing a Facebook article earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not a transaction with a ministry.
But if Christ has given you truth worth proclaiming, you can use what God has placed in your hands to point someone else toward Him.
It can carry the Gospel into the feed of someone who would never walk into a church.
Send it privately to the person you know is struggling.
Send it even to the skeptic who thinks Christianity is only about pretending to have everything together.
Scripture never gives us permission to make such claims.
But voluntary generosity, Gospel partnership, sharing biblical truth, and helping sound Christian resources reach others can genuinely be ways believers choose to glorify God.
Your support helps this kind of Christ-centered content continue reaching people who are scrolling through pain, temptation, doubt, loneliness, shame, and spiritual exhaustion.
Not as spiritual advertising.
As an invitation.
Because somewhere in your circle is a Samson.
Strong enough to fool everybody.
Successful enough to hide behind victories.
Smiling in photographs.
Functioning at work.
Showing up at church.
Answering, “I’m fine.”
And dying of thirst.
You may never know what God does with one article you were willing to share.
You may never know who reads it at 2:13 in the morning.
Who finally confesses.
Who finally calls someone for help.
Who opens a Bible again.
Who returns to church.
Who forgives.
Who repents.
Who falls to their knees.
Who realizes that Christianity was never about proving how strong they were.
It was about discovering how desperately they needed Christ.
Samson held the jawbone.
But the power was never ultimately in the jawbone.
And the deepest hope of Scripture was never Samson.
It was always moving toward Someone greater.
Jesus Christ.
The Deliverer who does not merely rescue us from enemies around us, but addresses the sin within us.
The Savior who knows every hidden chapter and still calls sinners to repentance.
The King who does not excuse our darkness but enters it with truth and grace.
The Lamb who was slain.
The Lord who rose.
The Christ who still saves.
So put down the performance.
Bring Him the thirst.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the failure.
Bring Him the appetite you cannot control.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the broken marriage.
Bring Him the exhausted faith.
Bring Him the version of you nobody else knows exists.
And repent.
Believe.
Follow Jesus.
Because the greatest miracle in Samson’s story was never meant to teach us that human beings can become strong enough to defeat everything.
It reminds us how desperately even the strongest among us need the power and mercy of God.
A thousand enemies may fall around you, but if your heart remains unsurrendered, the battle is not over.
And here is the line I hope follows you long after you close this article:
The strongest man in the room may still be the thirstiest soul in the room—and Jesus is still calling the thirsty to come to Him.
